From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>

Subject: Performance SLO qualification - latency & cost levers (follow-up)

Hi Ana / Tom —

Thanks again for the time this morning. Quick recap + next steps from our end so we can align on the simplest path to hit your UX targets.

What we heard you need:
- Latency: p95 <= 250ms for short, interactive responses (typical 40–120 tokens) and p95 <= 600ms for longer summarization responses (~400–600 tokens).
- Throughput & concurrency: average steady-state ~30 req/s, peak bursts to ~120 req/s, and up to ~150 concurrent active sessions during peak clinic hours.
- Streaming: required for your patient-facing chat UI (low time-to-first-token is important).
- Availability/compliance: SOC2 and audit logs required; no raw patient data leaves your VPC for Private deployments.

Initial cost constraint: you mentioned a roadmap budget target of ~$10k–20k/mo for inference (we can refine).

Cost/performance levers we discussed (attached PDF goes into more detail):
- Continuous batching: increases throughput efficiency for background workloads while still meeting interactive SLOs via adaptive small-window batching.
- Prefix/KV caching: reusing cached KV state for repeated prompts (e.g., clinical templates, standard system prompts).
- Model variants + quantization: use a smaller quantized model for routine responses (4-bit/QLoRA-style) and a higher-capacity model for long-form summarization; fallback policies for correctness-sensitive flows.
- Streaming optimizations: early token commit and prioritized scheduling to reduce TTF first-byte latency.

Ask from you (action items):
1) Share a simple traffic sample (CSV or 2–3 example sessions) showing tokens/request distribution and typical session length.
2) Confirm whether PHI will be present in requests or if you will token-redact client-side.
3) Any hard budget ceilings we must keep to?

Attached: SLO_worksheet_Orchid.xlsx (worksheet to fill with p95/p99 targets by endpoint) and redwood-performance-levers.pdf.

Proposed next step: Technical deep-dive with Rishi (runtime performance) and Vivek (capacity/cost) — can we do Wed 2/18 10:00am PT?

Thanks,
Marissa

marissa@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0126

Thanks Marissa — helpful recap. A few clarifications from our end:

- The bulk of our interactions are short (single-question triage + 1–2 sentence guidance): average response ~120 tokens; long-form summaries (discharge summaries) are ~450–600 tokens but less frequent (<5% of calls).
- Concurrency: we typically see 100–150 concurrent active users in peak windows (confirming your number).
- Streaming: yes, streaming is required for the patient chat experience (TFF is important; anything >300ms for first byte feels sluggish to clinicians).
- PHI: yes, requests will contain PHI. We will require Private deployment with our own VPC and KMS.
- Budget: our initial allocation for inference is closer to $15k/mo; flexible if tradeoffs are clear.

Happy to share a redacted sample traffic CSV — attaching a small extract (redacted_traffic_sample.csv).

Wed 2/18 10:00am PT works for a technical deep-dive. Please send invite and any prep materials you want us to review.

Ana — great, thanks for the sample and for confirming PHI requirements. A few notes ahead of the Wed deep-dive so we can make the session actionable: 

1) What we'll benchmark in the deep-dive:
   - Latency microbenchmarks for short responses (40–150 tokens) and long summaries (~500 tokens) across 2 model families (quantized Mistral-like 7B and a 13B baseline).
   - Streaming TTF (time-to-first-token) and sustained throughput under target concurrency.

2) Cost/performance levers we recommend (summary):
   - Continuous batching + adaptive tail latency windows: keeps per-token cost down while preserving p95 latency for interactive flows.
   - KV/prefix caching: impactful if you have repeated templates or system prompts; can cut compute by ~15–40% for those flows.
   - Model split: route high-frequency short replies to a quantized 7B variant and long summaries to a higher-capacity 13B/14B model (with cached contexts to avoid re-computation).
   - Quantization caveat: 4-bit quantization gives large cost savings but can change output characteristics for some safety-sensitive prompts — we recommend evals on a sample prompt set.

3) Prep asked of Orchid (before Wed):
   - Confirm tokens/request distribution (you sent a useful sample — thank you).
   - Fill the attached SLO_worksheet_Orchid.xlsx where possible.

4) Proposed agenda for Wed 2/18 10:00am PT (30–45m):
   - 10m: runbook & SLO alignment
   - 15m: runtime demo + microbenchmarks (Rishi)
   - 10m: capacity/cost estimate (Vivek)
   - 10m: next steps / rollout plan

I will send a calendar invite with a link to the shared Drive (drive folder includes the worksheet + our short technical note on quantization tradeoffs).

Thanks — looking forward to the deep-dive.
Marissa
